headings.title: Principles of Infant Feeding in HIV
headings.content: Infant feeding in the context of human immunodeficiency virus involves balancing the nutritional and immunological benefits of breastfeeding against the risk of vertical transmission. The primary goal is to maximize the child's chances of HIV-free survival while minimizing postnatal transmission through breast milk. Transmission can occur during pregnancy, labor, delivery, or breastfeeding. Without interventions, the overall risk of mother-to-child transmission ranges from fifteen to forty-five percent. When mothers adhere strictly to antiretroviral therapy and maintain an undetectable viral load, this transmission risk drops significantly. Clinical guidelines in many resource-limited settings, including Nigeria, emphasize continuous maternal antiretroviral therapy to enable safe breastfeeding, supporting both child health and maternal well-being.

headings.title: World Health Organization Recommendations
headings.content: Current global health standards empower HIV-positive mothers to breastfeed exclusively for the first six months of life, provided they are receiving lifelong antiretroviral therapy. After six months, appropriate complementary foods should be introduced alongside continued breastfeeding for up to twelve months or longer. This recommendation represents a shift from earlier practices that universally discouraged breastfeeding in favor of replacement feeding, which frequently led to high rates of malnutrition and diarrheal diseases in environments lacking safe water. National health policies adapt these global recommendations to local epidemiological realities, ensuring that mothers receive the structural support needed for successful viral suppression before initiating lactation.

headings.title: Exclusive Breastfeeding and Maternal Antiretroviral Therapy
headings.content:
Exclusive breastfeeding means the infant receives only breast milk without any additional liquids, water, or food items. When combined with maternal antiretroviral therapy, this practice significantly reduces viral load in breast milk, thereby lowering transmission risks. 

- **Adherence**: Consistent daily medication intake is mandatory to maintain viral suppression.
- **Infant Prophylaxis**: The baby often receives daily nevirapine or zidovudine syrup for the first six weeks of life as an added layer of defense.
- **Breast Health**: Prompt treatment of mastitis or cracked nipples is critical, as localized inflammation increases viral shedding in milk.

Mothers must understand that partial feeding carries higher risks than exclusive feeding due to mucosal damage from other foods.

headings.title: Replacement Feeding Safety and Preparation
headings.content:
When replacement feeding is chosen, it must be acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable, and safe, often remembered by the acronym AFASS. If any of these conditions are missing, replacement feeding poses a severe threat to infant survival due to malnutrition and severe infections.

| Condition | Clinical Consideration |
| --- | --- |
| Acceptable | No cultural barriers or stigma attached to formula use |
| Feasible | Mother has time, knowledge, and support to prepare formula |
| Affordable | Family can procure sufficient formula for the entire first year |
| Safe | Access to clean water, reliable fuel, and proper hygiene facilities |

Preparation requires scrupulous hygiene, including boiling water and sterilizing feeding utensils to prevent fatal gastroenteritis.

headings.title: Mixed Feeding Risks and Prevention
headings.content: Mixed feeding—giving breast milk alongside water, formula, or other foods before six months of age—is strongly discouraged for mothers with HIV. Introducing non-human milk or solids damages the delicate mucosal lining of the infant's immature gastrointestinal tract. This microscopic inflammation creates easy entry points for the virus present in breast milk to cross into the bloodstream. Consequently, infants who are mixed-fed face a significantly higher rate of HIV transmission compared to those who are exclusively breastfed or exclusively formula-fed. Healthcare counseling must actively address cultural pressures that encourage early water or food supplementation.

headings.title: Transition to Complementary Foods
headings.content: At six months of age, breast milk alone no longer satisfies the growing infant's nutritional requirements for energy and micronutrients. Complementary foods must be introduced gradually while continuing breastfeeding up to one year or beyond, depending on local guidelines. Foods should be nutrient-dense, rich in iron and protein, and prepared under strict hygienic conditions. As solid food intake increases, breastfeeding frequency may naturally decrease, but complete cessation should only occur when a nutritionally adequate and safe diet can be provided without breast milk.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Counseling
headings.content: Nurses play a pivotal role in supporting HIV-positive mothers through empathetic, non-judgmental counseling. Assessment involves evaluating the mother's viral load suppression status, mental health, household support structures, and infant feeding intentions. Counseling must be continuous rather than a single event, starting during antenatal visits and extending through the postnatal period. Nurses should address stigma, provide practical demonstrations on safe formula preparation or expressing and heat-treating breast milk if needed, and reinforce medication adherence to protect both mother and child.
